title: The Ayyubid Sultanate
subtitle: 1171–1250 · Saladin's Confederation, the Sunnisation of Egypt and the Crusades

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Not a line of kings but a family — Saladin, the sultans of Egypt who followed him, and the co-equal Ayyubid princes of Syria and the Jazira

entries.label: Saladin welds Egypt and Syria into one bloc
entries.hint: Sent to Egypt as a Zangid officer, Saladin made himself vizier in 1169, ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, and on Nur al-Din's death in 1174 marched on Syria. Over twelve years he took Damascus, Homs and Hama, forced Aleppo to terms in 1183 and the lord of Mosul to homage in 1186, ringing the Crusader states with a single Sunni power. The Abbasid caliph recognised him as sultan.
entries.note: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, 'al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya', is an eyewitness but wrote as Saladin's own qadi and admirer; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, his secretary, writes ornate partisan rhymed prose; Ibn al-Athir, from Mosul, is cool toward Saladin out of Zangid loyalty and is the necessary corrective. Lyons and Jackson, 'Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War' (1982), triangulates them.

entries.label: Saladin — the reconquest and the last years
entries.hint: Hattin in July 1187 destroyed the field army of the kingdom of Jerusalem; the holy city and most of the coast followed within the year. The Third Crusade clawed back a coastal strip, and the truce of 1192 left Saladin the interior and Jerusalem. He died at Damascus in March 1193 with almost no money of his own, the realm already parcelled among some seventeen sons, brothers and nephews.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad is closest for 1188–93 (he was in Saladin's camp); the Frankish side is in the 'Itinerarium Peregrinorum' and Ambroise. On the division of the realm: Humphreys, 'From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193–1260' (1977), the standard study of the whole dynasty.

entries.label: The war of Saladin's heirs and the rise of al-Adil
entries.hint: Saladin's sons at once fell out — al-Afdal in Damascus, al-Aziz Uthman in Cairo, al-Zahir in Aleppo — and campaigned against one another for seven years. Their uncle al-Adil, Saladin's brother and long his chief lieutenant, played the nephews off, and by 1200 held Egypt and the senior sultanate himself.
entries.note: Humphreys (1977), chs. 3–4; Ibn Wasil, 'Mufarrij al-Kurub', an Ayyubid loyalist writing under the Mamluks, is the fullest connected narrative and must be read for that sympathy.

entries.label: Al-Adil reunites the confederation
entries.hint: A careful administrator and negotiator who preferred truce and trade with the Franks to holy war, al-Adil (the Franks called him Saphadin) held the whole confederation under his hand while parcelling its provinces among his own sons: al-Kamil in Egypt, al-Mu'azzam in Damascus, al-Ashraf in the Jazira. He died in 1218 as the Fifth Crusade landed at Damietta.
entries.note: Humphreys (1977); al-Adil's long series of commercial treaties with Venice and Pisa survive in the Italian archives and are near-primary evidence for his policy.

entries.label: Al-Kamil
entries.hint: Al-Kamil beat the Fifth Crusade at Mansura in 1221, ceded an unwalled Jerusalem to Frederick II by treaty in 1229, and spent twenty years at war with his brothers al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf for control of Syria. He briefly reunited Egypt and Damascus in 1238 and died weeks later.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil (who knew al-Kamil's court personally); Humphreys (1977); the Frankish and papal sources for the 1229 treaty, hostile to a deal made with an excommunicate emperor.

entries.label: Al-Salih Ayyub and rule by mamluk
entries.hint: Al-Salih Ayyub seized Egypt from his brother in 1240 and ruled by fear, leaning on a regiment of purchased Qipchaq Turks — the Bahriyya, quartered in a new barracks on Rawda island — and on a corps of stateless Khwarazmian horsemen who sacked Jerusalem for him in 1244. He recovered Damascus in 1245 and died at Mansura in November 1249 as Louis IX invaded.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil; al-Maqrizi's 'Suluk' (15th c., for the Egyptian administrative detail); the rise of the Bahriyya is reconstructed in Humphreys (1977) and Ayalon's studies of the mamluk institution.

entries.label: Turanshah, Shajar al-Durr and the Mamluk seizure
entries.hint: Al-Salih's widow Shajar al-Durr concealed his death to hold the front against Louis IX. His son al-Mu'azzam Turanshah arrived from the Jazira, completed the defeat of the French — then alienated the Bahriyya, who cut him down at Fariskur in May 1250. The slave-soldiers took the state; the Ayyubid line in Egypt was finished.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil and al-Maqrizi; John of Joinville's 'Life of Saint Louis' is an eyewitness to the campaign and to Turanshah's murder, seen from the French prisoners' camp. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's coup entry.

entries.label: The lesser principalities — Hama, Homs, the Jazira and Yemen
entries.hint: A scatter of family holdings owed loose allegiance to whichever sultan was strongest: Hama, where the princes and the later historian-ruler Abu al-Fida made a cultural centre and which survived as a Mamluk vassal until 1341; Homs and Baalbek; Mayyafariqin and Hisn Kayfa in the Jazira; and Yemen, held from Turanshah's conquest in 1174 until the Rasulids succeeded the Ayyubids there as independent rulers in 1229.
entries.note: Humphreys (1977); for Yemen, the chronicle of Umara al-Yamani and Smith, 'The Ayyubids and Early Rasulids in the Yemen' (1974–78).

entries.label: The Aleppo line
entries.hint: Al-Zahir Ghazi, Saladin's son, and then al-Aziz Muhammad ruled the rich principality of north Syria as the most autonomous Ayyubid branch — rebuilding the citadel of Aleppo, patronising scholars, keeping their own foreign policy. The line ended when al-Nasir Yusuf, who had reunited Aleppo and Damascus, was swept away by the Mongols in 1260.
entries.note: Eddé, 'La principauté ayyoubide d'Alep (579/1183–658/1260)' (1999), the definitive study; Ibn al-Adim's 'Bughya' and 'Zubda', the local Aleppo chronicles and biographical dictionary, near-primary.

entries.label: The Damascus line
entries.hint: Damascus passed among Saladin's and al-Adil's descendants. Al-Mu'azzam Isa (1218–1227) slighted Jerusalem's walls to deny the city to any future crusade and allied with the Khwarazm-Shah against his own kin; then came al-Ashraf, al-Salih Ismail — who offered the Franks Palestinian fortresses for help against Egypt — and finally al-Nasir Yusuf.
entries.note: Humphreys, 'From Saladin to the Mongols' (1977), is built around the Damascus sultanate; Ibn al-Qalanisi's chronicle ends in 1160 but his continuators and Abu Shama's 'Dhayl' carry the thread.

entries.label: The end of the dynasty in Syria
entries.hint: With Egypt lost to the mamluks, al-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo and Damascus was the last Ayyubid of weight. He temporised with both the Mamluks and the Mongols until Hulagu stormed Aleppo and occupied Damascus in 1260 and had him killed. Ayn Jalut that year left Syria to the Mamluks; only tiny Hama lingered on.
entries.note: Ibn al-Adim (who fled Aleppo before the sack); Bar Hebraeus, the Syriac chronicler, contemporary and writing across the confessional divide; the Mongol side in Juvayni and later Rashid al-Din. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Hattin and the recovery of Jerusalem, three crusades aimed at Egypt, the wars within the family, and the Mongol onset

entries.label: Hattin
entries.loc: the Horns of Hattin, above Tiberias
entries.hint: Lured into the waterless plateau west of the Sea of Galilee, the field army of the kingdom of Jerusalem was surrounded and destroyed on 4 July 1187. Saladin captured King Guy, Reynald of Chatillon (whom he killed with his own hand) and the relic of the True Cross. The kingdom had almost no one left to hold its castles.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Shaddad on the Muslim side; the 'Libellus de expugnatione Terrae Sanctae' and the Old French continuations of William of Tyre on the Frankish. The reconstruction of the battlefield movements: Kedar in 'The Horns of Hattin' (1992).

entries.label: The surrender of Jerusalem
entries.hint: After a short siege Balian of Ibelin negotiated terms: the Christian population was ransomed, not massacred — the deliberate inversion of the Crusader conduct of 1099 was noticed on both sides. Saladin had the Haram al-Sharif cleansed of its Crusader additions and brought Nur al-Din's carved minbar into al-Aqsa.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad; Imad al-Din, who was present; the Frankish accounts stress the numbers left unransomed and enslaved. The minbar was destroyed by arson in 1969.

entries.label: The siege of Acre
entries.hint: The released King Guy laid siege to Acre; Saladin then besieged the besiegers, and the two armies locked around the city for two years. The arrival of Philip II of France and Richard I of England broke the deadlock; the garrison surrendered, and when the agreed ransom stalled Richard had some 2,700 prisoners killed within sight of Saladin's lines.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad (an eyewitness to the massacre from the Muslim camp); Ambroise and the 'Itinerarium' for the Crusader account, which justifies the killing. Gillingham, 'Richard I' (1999), on the episode.

entries.label: Arsuf, the marches on Jerusalem and the Treaty of Jaffa
entries.hint: Richard beat Saladin in a pitched fight at Arsuf and rebuilt the coastal defences, but twice advanced toward Jerusalem and twice judged it impossible to hold and turned back. The truce of September 1192 gave the Franks the coast from Tyre to Jaffa and pilgrim access to the holy places; Saladin kept the city.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad; Ambroise. The strategic argument over whether Jerusalem could be held is set out in both traditions and is analysed by Smail, 'Crusading Warfare' (1956).

entries.label: The wars of Saladin's house
entries.hint: For seven years after Saladin's death his sons and brother fought openly for the inheritance — campaigns around Damascus, in the Jordan valley and into Egypt — while the Franks, exhausted themselves, mostly watched. The fighting settled only when al-Adil had gathered Egypt, Damascus and the Jazira into his own hands.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Wasil; Humphreys, 'From Saladin to the Mongols' (1977), chs. 3–4.

entries.label: Al-Kamil against his brothers
entries.hint: The confederation nearly came apart in a generation of wars among al-Kamil in Egypt, al-Mu'azzam in Damascus and al-Ashraf in the Jazira. Al-Mu'azzam allied with the Khwarazm-Shah Jalal al-Din against his own family; al-Kamil's readiness to hand Jerusalem to Frederick II in 1229 was in part a bid for a Frankish counterweight against Damascus.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil; Humphreys (1977). The link between the family war and the 1229 treaty is drawn out by Hamilton, 'The Leper King and his Heirs' notwithstanding — see rather Gabrieli, 'Arab Historians of the Crusades' (1969), for the Arabic reaction to the deal.

entries.label: Damietta
entries.hint: The Crusaders took Damietta after an eighteen-month siege. Al-Kamil three times offered Jerusalem and the True Cross for their withdrawal; the papal legate Pelagius refused each time. The army then marched on Cairo, was trapped between the Nile and its flood channels at Mansura, and surrendered Damietta to be allowed to leave.
entries.note: Oliver of Paderborn, an eyewitness on the Crusader side; Ibn Wasil and al-Maqrizi for the Egyptian. Powell, 'Anatomy of a Crusade 1213–1221' (1986), is the standard modern account and weighs al-Kamil's peace offers.

entries.label: The 1229 cession of Jerusalem and the Muslim reaction
entries.hint: By the Treaty of Jaffa al-Kamil handed Frederick II the city of Jerusalem — unwalled, with the Haram left in Muslim hands — for a ten-year truce. Frederick crowned himself in the Holy Sepulchre. Preachers denounced the deal from the pulpits of Damascus and Cairo, and the Damascus Ayyubids repudiated it.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil (who later met Frederick's son Manfred as an envoy and admired the Hohenstaufen court); the Arabic sermons and reactions in Sibt ibn al-Jawzi. The Frankish clergy were equally hostile to a treaty with an excommunicate.

entries.label: Köse Dagh, the tributary Jazira and the fall of Syria
entries.loc: Köse Dagh, near Sivas; Aleppo; Damascus
entries.hint: The Mongols crushed the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dagh in 1243, removing the buffer to the north and making the Jaziran Ayyubid principalities tributary. In 1260 Hulagu took Aleppo by storm and occupied Damascus, ending Ayyubid rule in Syria. The Mamluk victory at Ayn Jalut that year halted the advance but did not bring the dynasty back.
entries.note: Bar Hebraeus and Ibn al-Adim for Aleppo; the Mongol campaign in Juvayni (in Hulagu's service) and later Rashid al-Din. Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks: The Mamluk-Ilkhanid War 1260–1281' (1995).

entries.label: The Khwarazmian sack of Jerusalem and La Forbie
entries.hint: Al-Salih Ayyub hired the stateless Khwarazmian cavalry; in the summer of 1244 they stormed Jerusalem, wrecked the church of the Holy Sepulchre and drove out the Christians — the city stayed in Muslim hands until 1917. Weeks later the joint Egyptian and Khwarazmian army annihilated the allied Frankish and Damascene host at La Forbie, a defeat as total as Hattin and the last great pitched battle of crusader history.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil; the Rothelin continuation of William of Tyre and Matthew Paris on the Frankish side. Jackson, 'The Crusades of 1239–41 and their Aftermath', BSOAS (1987), on the battle and its scale.

entries.label: Louis IX at Damietta and Mansura
entries.hint: Louis IX of France took an undefended Damietta in June 1249. Al-Salih Ayyub died as the French pushed inland; at Mansura, Robert of Artois led a charge into the town and was killed, and the army was then blockaded on the river, starved, struck by disease and forced to surrender. Louis was ransomed for Damietta and 400,000 livres.
entries.note: John of Joinville, who was there and captured with the king — the fullest eyewitness account of any crusade; Ibn Wasil and al-Maqrizi for the Egyptian side and the role of the Bahriyya in the victory.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A change of state religion carried out from the top, the family confederation as a constitutional form, the iqta, and the re-Islamisation of Jerusalem

entries.label: The Sunni restoration of Egypt in law
entries.hint: Saladin abolished the Ismaili courts and the Shi'i formula in the call to prayer, restored Sunni qadis of all four schools, converted the Fatimid palace colleges to Sunni teaching, endowed the first Sunni madrasas in Cairo and Fustat, and returned the Friday prayer to the name of the Abbasid caliph. The state religion of Egypt was changed from the top in under a decade.
entries.note: Leiser, 'The Restoration of Sunnism in Egypt: Madrasas and Mudarrisun 495–647/1101–1249' (PhD 1976) and his articles; al-Maqrizi's 'Khitat' lists the foundations. The near-total absence of resistance is itself the evidence that Fatimid Egypt had stayed Sunni.

entries.label: The dhimma under the Ayyubids
entries.hint: Christians and Jews stayed in the fiscal bureaucracy and dominated the medical profession, but the Ayyubids ran a harder line than the Fatimids: the non-Muslim vizier disappears, dress rules and dismissals from office were enforced in waves, and the pressure grew through the 1240s and 1250s. It is the start of the long contraction of the Coptic administrative class.
entries.note: the 'History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria' (a contemporary Coptic chronicle); the Geniza for the Jewish side (Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society', 1967–93). Yarbrough, 'Friends of the Emir' (2019), on the recurring campaigns against non-Muslim officials.

entries.label: Ayyubid coinage and the last figural dirhams
entries.hint: The gold dinar was debased and struck irregularly as West African gold flowed west toward the Almohads; the silver dirham became the real money of account. Meanwhile the Jaziran Ayyubid and neighbouring Artuqid mints kept striking large figural copper coins — classical heads, zodiac signs, enthroned rulers — the last sustained tradition of images on Islamic coins.
entries.note: Balog, 'The Coinage of the Ayyubids' (1980); Spengler and Sayles, 'Turko-Iranian Coins and their Iconography' vol. 1 (1992), on the Jaziran figural types.

entries.label: The iqta and the cadastral survey
entries.hint: The Ayyubids took over and tightened the Fatimid military iqta: an officer held the tax revenue of assigned villages in return for keeping a fixed number of armoured horsemen. Al-Kamil had Egypt re-surveyed (the rawk) around 1218. The free peasantry and the cash economy contracted further under the system.
entries.note: Cahen, 'L'évolution de l'iqta du IXe au XIIIe siècle', Annales (1953); Rabie, 'The Financial System of Egypt AH 564–741 / AD 1169–1341' (1972), the standard treatment of Ayyubid and early Mamluk fiscality.

entries.label: The confederation as a form of government
entries.hint: The Ayyubid realm was held as family property: divided among the adult males, each a near-sovereign in his own city, owing the senior sultan military aid and the mention of his name in the Friday sermon and on the coinage. Under a strong figure — Saladin, al-Adil — it worked; otherwise it tipped into civil war. It was the structural weakness the Mamluks replaced with a unitary state.
entries.note: Humphreys, 'From Saladin to the Mongols' (1977), esp. the introduction and conclusion; Chamberlain, 'Knowledge and Social Practice in Medieval Damascus' (1994), on how appanage politics shaped the city.

entries.label: The re-Islamisation of Jerusalem
entries.hint: After 1187 Saladin reversed 88 years of Frankish Christian Jerusalem: the Templar and Hospitaller additions to the Haram were removed, al-Aqsa and the Dome of the Rock reconsecrated, a madrasa and a khanqah founded within the walls, and Jews permitted to resettle the city for the first time since 1099.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad; the Jewish resettlement in the Geniza and in Judah al-Harizi's account of his visit c.1216. Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999), ch. 5, on the Islamic re-consecration.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Egypt returns to Sunni Islam, the madrasa and the khanqah become organs of state, Ibn Arabi in Damascus, and Maimonides at the head of the Jews of Egypt

entries.label: The Sunni triumph in Egypt
entries.hint: After 260 years of Ismaili rule Egypt returned to the Sunni fold with almost no friction, because the Fatimid da'wa had never converted the population. The Ayyubids planted Shafi'i and Maliki madrasas, installed a Shafi'i chief qadi, and pushed the surviving Ismaili missionary organisation underground or out to Yemen and, later, India.
entries.note: Leiser (1976) and his 'The Madrasa and the Islamization of the Middle East', JARCE (1985); the emigration of the Musta'li da'wa to Yemen is traced in Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2nd ed. 2007). Cross-references the Fatimid folio.

entries.label: Maimonides, head of the Jews of Egypt
entries.hint: A refugee from Almohad persecution in the west, Musa ibn Maymun settled in Fustat, served as a physician to Saladin's vizier al-Qadi al-Fadil and to the household of Saladin's son al-Afdal, and was recognised as head of the Jews. Here he completed the 'Mishneh Torah', wrote the 'Guide of the Perplexed', and sent the 'Epistle to Yemen'. The pre-eminent Jewish thinker of the Middle Ages did his work under Ayyubid rule.
entries.note: Maimonides' letters and responsa, many preserved in the Cairo Geniza in his own hand; Kraemer, 'Maimonides: The Life and World of One of Civilization's Greatest Minds' (2008).

entries.label: Sufism becomes an institution of state
entries.hint: In 1173 Saladin endowed the khanqah of Sa'id al-Su'ada in Cairo — the first state-funded Sufi lodge in Egypt, with a salaried shaykh al-shuyukh and a residency of dervishes. His successors multiplied khanqahs across Egypt and Syria. Organised, endowed Sufism moved in this period from the margins to the centre of religious life.
entries.note: the group label here marks a new religious institution, not a mission; al-Maqrizi's 'Khitat' on the Sa'id al-Su'ada. Hofer, 'The Popularisation of Sufism in Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt' (2015), is the study.

entries.label: The four-madhhab madrasa and Ash'ari theology
entries.hint: The Ayyubid madrasa taught one or more of the four Sunni law schools with Ash'ari theology and al-Ghazali's synthesis as the norm. Al-Salih Ayyub's Salihiyya of 1242 was the first foundation in Egypt to endow chairs in all four schools at once and the first dedicated dar al-hadith. This is the institutional mould of Sunni orthodoxy for the next several centuries.
entries.note: Leiser (1976); Berkey, 'The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo' (1992), for the social workings of the madrasa; the Salihiyya endowment deed is partly preserved.

entries.label: The Hanbali migration to Salihiyya
entries.hint: A community of Hanbali scholars from the hills near Nablus — the Banu Qudama — displaced by Frankish pressure, took root in the Salihiyya suburb of Damascus and were consolidated there under Ayyubid patronage. Muwaffaq al-Din ibn Qudama's 'al-Mughni' became the great Hanbali law manual. The Damascus Hanbali school that later produced Ibn Taymiyya grew from this settlement.
entries.note: Diya al-Din al-Maqdisi's account of the community's migration is a near-primary local source; Talmon-Heller, 'Islamic Piety in Medieval Syria' (2007), on the Banu Qudama and Ayyubid religious life.

entries.label: The Coptic golden age of Arabic letters
entries.hint: Even as the community shrank and came under fiscal pressure, Coptic scholarship in Arabic reached its height. The three Awlad al-Assal brothers compiled the standard Coptic canon law, a critical edition of the Arabic Gospels and Coptic-Arabic lexica; theology, history and the Coptic encyclopaedic tradition were all written under the Ayyubids.
entries.note: the works of al-Safi, al-As'ad and al-Mu'taman ibn al-Assal; Sidarus's studies of the Copto-Arabic renaissance; the 'History of the Patriarchs' as a running contemporary source.

entries.label: Ibn Arabi and the unity of being, in Damascus
entries.hint: The Andalusi mystic Ibn Arabi, later called al-Shaykh al-Akbar, spent his last seventeen years under Ayyubid protection in Damascus, completing the vast 'Meccan Openings' and writing the 'Bezels of Wisdom'. The doctrine later summarised as wahdat al-wujud, the oneness of being, became the common idiom of later Islamic mysticism and its greatest theological controversy. He is buried at Salihiyya.
entries.note: Ibn Arabi's own works; Addas, 'Quest for the Red Sulphur: The Life of Ibn Arabi' (1993); Chittick, 'The Sufi Path of Knowledge' (1989). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's Ibn Arabi entry.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Citadel of Cairo, the tomb-madrasa, the great citadels of Syria, inlaid brass and enamelled glass

entries.label: Enamelled glass and Raqqa ware
entries.hint: The Syrian glasshouses brought gilded and enamelled glass to maturity under the Ayyubids — the mosque lamps and beakers that medieval Europe prized and imitated — while the kilns of Raqqa and Damascus turned out lustre and underglaze-painted pottery in quantity.
entries.note: Carboni, 'Glass from Islamic Lands' (2001); the debate over the 'Raqqa' attribution (Jenkins-Madina, 'Raqqa Revisited', 2006).

entries.label: The Citadel of Cairo
entries.hint: Saladin began the fortress on the Muqattam spur to bring Cairo and Fustat under one wall; al-Kamil finished it and made it the seat of government. With its deep well, its mosques and its palaces, the Citadel was the residence of every ruler of Egypt from the 13th century until 1874.
entries.note: Creswell, 'The Muslim Architecture of Egypt' vol. 2 (1959); the building inscriptions of Saladin's brother al-Adil and of al-Kamil survive on the walls and towers.

entries.label: The poets of the Ayyubid courts
entries.hint: Baha al-Din Zuhayr served al-Salih Ayyub as court poet and chancery head and wrote a clear, graceful diwan admired ever since; Ibn Sana al-Mulk revived the Andalusi muwashshah form in Egypt and theorised it; and the chancery prose of al-Qadi al-Fadil, Saladin's secretary, was studied as a model for centuries.
entries.note: the diwans of Baha al-Din Zuhayr (trans. E. H. Palmer, 1876–77) and Ibn Sana al-Mulk; al-Fadil's letters, much quoted by Imad al-Din and Abu Shama.

entries.label: The citadels of Syria and the ablaq facade
entries.hint: Al-Zahir Ghazi's rebuilding of the citadel of Aleppo — the glacis, the great gate-block, the throne hall — is among the finest fortresses of the medieval world. The Ayyubids also raised or rebuilt Damascus, Bosra, Ajlun, Harran and Sahyun, and in their Syrian buildings developed the striped light-and-dark stone courses (ablaq) and the honeycomb muqarnas portal that became the signature of Mamluk architecture.
entries.note: Tabbaa, 'Constructions of Power and Piety in Medieval Aleppo' (1997); the archaeological survey of the Aleppo citadel published after 2000.

entries.label: Inlaid brass and the scattering of Mosul
entries.hint: Ayyubid Syria and the Jazira produced silver- and gold-inlaid brass basins, ewers and boxes of exceptional refinement, some carrying Christian Gospel scenes made for Muslim or Christian buyers (the Freer canteen, the d'Arenberg basin). Metalworkers trained in Mosul dispersed into the Ayyubid cities as the Mongols closed in.
entries.note: Ward, 'Islamic Metalwork' (1993); Baer, 'Ayyubid Metalwork with Christian Images' (1989).

entries.label: The tomb-madrasa arrives in Egypt
entries.hint: The cruciform four-iwan madrasa came to Egypt from Syria and Iraq under the Ayyubids. Al-Salih Ayyub's Salihiyya of 1242, with its surviving minaret, and the domed tomb his widow built for him beside it in 1250 — the first royal mausoleum on a Cairo street — began the avenue of tomb-madrasas that the Mamluks would fill for 250 years.
entries.note: Creswell vol. 2 (1959); Humphreys, 'The Expressive Intent of the Mamluk Architecture of Cairo', Studia Islamica (1972), traces the Ayyubid origin of the type.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Maimonides in Fustat, Abd al-Latif's observation against Galen, al-Suhrawardi and the philosophy of light, and the competing historians of Saladin

entries.label: Ayyubid medicine and the teaching hospital
entries.hint: The Nuri hospital of Damascus, founded by Nur al-Din, became under the Ayyubids the leading medical school of the Near East; al-Dahwar endowed a dedicated medical madrasa attached to it. Ibn al-Nafis, who would describe the passage of the blood through the lungs, trained at the Nuri before moving to Cairo. The Nasiri hospital, installed in the old Fatimid palace, served Cairo.
entries.note: Ibn Abi Usaybia's 'Uyun al-Anba', the biographical dictionary of physicians, is contemporary and was compiled in this milieu. Ibn al-Nafis's mature career and the pulmonary-transit passage fall under early Mamluk rule — flag the Mamluk folio.

entries.label: Al-Suhrawardi and the philosophy of illumination
entries.hint: Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi built the ishraqi, or illuminationist, system — recasting Avicennan philosophy around a hierarchy of lights and a theory of knowledge by direct presence. He was put to death at Aleppo in 1191, aged about 38, on Saladin's order at the urging of the city's jurists and his son al-Zahir. Known thereafter as al-Maqtul, the killed one, he nonetheless shaped later Persian philosophy down to Mulla Sadra.
entries.note: the 'Hikmat al-Ishraq', trans. Walbridge and Ziai (1999); Ziai, 'Knowledge and Illumination' (1990). The execution shows the limits Ayyubid orthodoxy set on falsafa.

entries.label: Maimonides and the Guide of the Perplexed
entries.hint: Written in Judaeo-Arabic, the 'Guide of the Perplexed' set out to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with the Torah; through its Hebrew and Latin translations it shaped Jewish, Christian and some Muslim thought for centuries. Maimonides' letter on astrology, denying that the stars govern human affairs, is a landmark of medieval scientific scepticism.
entries.note: the 'Guide', ed. and trans. Pines (1963); the astrology letter to the rabbis of southern France. Cross-references the belief entry on Maimonides as head of the Jewish community.

entries.label: Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi — observation against authority
entries.hint: The Baghdad polymath taught at Saladin's Jerusalem and then in Cairo, Damascus and Aleppo. His 'Book of Instruction and Admonition on the Things Seen in Egypt' describes the great famine of 1200–1202 at first hand and, from examining the bones of the dead, corrects Galen on the anatomy of the lower jaw and the sacrum — direct inspection overruling the ancient authority.
entries.note: the 'Kitab al-Ifada wal-Itibar', trans. Zand and Videan, 'The Eastern Key' (1965); Abd al-Latif's autobiography, preserved by Ibn Abi Usaybia, is a rare first-person scholarly life.

entries.label: The historians of Saladin and the Ayyubids
entries.hint: The age produced an unusually rich and openly competing set of histories: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, Saladin's own qadi and eyewitness; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, his chancery secretary, in ornate rhymed prose; the Mosuli Ibn al-Athir, cool toward Saladin out of Zangid loyalty; Abu Shama of Damascus, who compiled the earlier writers; and Ibn Wasil, the fullest Ayyubid chronicle, completed under the Mamluks.
entries.note: the source-critical problem is the subject of Gabrieli, 'Arab Historians of the Crusades' (1969), intro., and of Hirschler, 'Medieval Arabic Historiography' (2006). Each writer's position has to be weighed.

entries.label: Yaqut al-Hamawi and the encyclopedists
entries.hint: A manumitted slave of Greek origin, Yaqut compiled the 'Mu'jam al-Buldan', a vast alphabetical geography of the Islamic world, and the 'Irshad', a dictionary of scholars — working in Aleppo and Mosul after fleeing the first Mongol wave from Merv. Ibn al-Qifti, vizier of Aleppo, wrote his history of the learned in the same circle.
entries.note: the 'Mu'jam al-Buldan', ed. Wüstenfeld (1866–73); Yaqut's own account of the flight from Khurasan is embedded in the entries. Ibn al-Qifti, 'Tarikh al-Hukama'.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The Red Sea spice route and the Karimi merchants, the treaties with the Italian republics, the famine of 1200, sugar, and the militarised land

entries.label: The Red Sea route and the Karimi merchants
entries.hint: The Ayyubids taxed and protected the spice trade that ran from the Indian Ocean through Aden, up the Red Sea to Aydhab, overland to Qus and down the Nile to Cairo and Alexandria. In this period the Karimi — a recognisable corporation of long-distance spice financiers — emerge as the wealthiest merchants of the Islamic world.
entries.note: Goitein and Friedman, 'India Traders of the Middle Ages' (2008); Ashtor, 'The Karimi Merchants', JRAS (1956), and the revisions in Fischel and later work. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's Karimi entry.

entries.label: Sugar
entries.loc: the Egyptian Delta and the Jordan valley
entries.hint: Egypt and the Jordan valley were the Mediterranean's main sugar producers. Ayyubid mills — like the neighbouring Frankish ones — pressed and boiled cane for refining and export to Europe. The crop was capital-intensive and irrigation-hungry, and its finance tied it closely to the state and the military elite.
entries.note: Ashtor, 'Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages' (1983); the archaeology of the Jordan-valley sugar mills (Jones and others) and the Egyptian evidence in the Geniza.

entries.label: The treaties with the Italian republics
entries.hint: Al-Adil and al-Kamil granted Venice, Pisa and Genoa fixed tariffs, resident consuls and walled trading compounds (funduqs) in Alexandria. Egypt supplied alum for European cloth-dyeing, plus sugar, flax and pepper, against silver, timber and iron. The papal bans on selling war material to the Muslims were continuously evaded.
entries.note: the treaty texts survive in the Venetian and Pisan archives (Tafel and Thomas; Amari, 'I diplomi arabi'); Jacoby's studies of the Alexandria trade. The trade continued through every crusade.

entries.label: Yemen, Aden and the India trade
entries.hint: Turanshah's conquest of Yemen in 1174 gave the Ayyubids the customs house of Aden, the pivot where the Indian and Egyptian trades met and where duties were among the richest in the Islamic world. Even after the Rasulids succeeded the Ayyubids in Yemen in 1229, the Egypt–Aden–India axis defined Red Sea commerce.
entries.note: Margariti, 'Aden and the Indian Ocean Trade' (2007); the Rasulid administrative texts (the 'Nur al-Maarif') for the slightly later period; Smith, 'The Ayyubids and Early Rasulids in the Yemen' (1974–78).

entries.label: The militarised land and the shrinking of cash
entries.hint: The spread of the iqta, the army's direct claim on rural revenue, and the 13th-century shortage of good gold coin pushed the Ayyubid economy toward payment in kind and in assignment rather than cash. It is the pattern the Mamluk state would carry to its extreme.
entries.note: Rabie, 'The Financial System of Egypt' (1972); Cahen on the iqta. The gold shortage is part of a wider 13th-century eastern-Mediterranean pattern (Watson, 'Back to Gold and Silver', Economic History Review, 1967).

entries.label: The great famine of 1200–1202
entries.hint: A failed Nile flood followed by epidemic disease killed a large share of Egypt's population. Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi, in Cairo through it, recorded emptied villages, a collapsed food supply and, in the worst of it, cannibalism. It is a reminder that the whole Ayyubid fiscal machine rested on the annual flood.
entries.note: Abd al-Latif's eyewitness 'Kitab al-Ifada'; al-Maqrizi's later treatise on Egyptian famines, 'Ighathat al-Umma', sets it in a long series. Mortality figures in the sources are impressionistic.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The answer to the Crusader castle, al-Jazari's machines in the neighbouring Jazira, anatomy from the famine dead, and water for the fortress-cities

entries.label: The answer to the Crusader castle
entries.hint: Ayyubid military engineering absorbed and countered Frankish fortification: the bent entrance passage, the continuous machicolation, the sloping stone talus and the concentric enceinte appear or mature in the citadels of Ajlun, Aleppo, Bosra and Cairo. Ayyubid armies also fielded large trebuchet trains at the sieges of Acre and Damietta.
entries.note: the castle of Ajlun (Qalat al-Rabad), built 1184–85, is a well-dated Ayyubid example; Kennedy, 'Crusader Castles' (1994), and the survey literature on Aleppo and Bosra.

entries.label: Water for the Citadel and the Ghouta
entries.hint: The Ayyubids built the aqueduct carrying Nile water up to the Cairo Citadel (later raised by the Mamluks) and maintained and extended the canal and qanat network of the Ghouta oasis that made Damascus habitable. Keeping a fortress-city watered under siege conditions was itself a strategic technology.
entries.note: Creswell vol. 2 (1959) on the Cairo aqueduct's Ayyubid core; the Damascus water system in Sauvaget's and Élisséeff's studies of the medieval city.

entries.label: Anatomy from the famine dead
entries.hint: Examining the bones of the tens of thousands who died in the Egyptian famine, Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi established by direct inspection that the human lower jaw is a single bone and the sacrum normally a single fused mass — correcting Galen, who had taught otherwise. It is an isolated but striking case of observation, forced by circumstance, overruling textual authority.
entries.note: Abd al-Latif, 'Kitab al-Ifada wal-Itibar', trans. Zand and Videan (1965); the passage is discussed in Savage-Smith's work on Islamic anatomy and the limits of dissection.

entries.label: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Devices
entries.hint: At the Artuqid court of Amid — an Ayyubid neighbour and sometime vassal in the Jazira — Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari completed his illustrated treatise describing the crankshaft, the segmental gear, double-acting suction pumps, and water-clocks and serving-automata whose sequences could be reprogrammed. It is the fullest medieval account of working machinery.
entries.note: al-Jazari, 'al-Jami bayn al-Ilm wal-Amal', trans. Hill, 'The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices' (1974). The patronage is Artuqid, not Ayyubid — cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's al-Jazari entry.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The truce system with Outremer, al-Kamil and Frederick II, Usama ibn Munqidh's frontier world, the scholars fleeing the Mongols, and Saladin the European legend

entries.label: Usama ibn Munqidh and life across the frontier
entries.hint: The 'Book of Contemplation', the memoir of a Syrian gentleman-warrior who hunted, negotiated, doctored and dined with Franks as readily as he fought them, is the fullest first-hand Muslim picture of the Crusader Levant as a lived-in mixed society rather than a front line.
entries.note: Usama ibn Munqidh, 'Kitab al-Itibar', trans. Cobb, 'The Book of Contemplation' (2008). Usama wrote in old age at the Ayyubid court and shaped his anecdotes to entertain and instruct — read as literature as much as report.

entries.label: Saladin becomes a European legend
entries.hint: Within a lifetime Western writers had turned Saladin into a model of chivalry: the tale of his knighting by a Frankish lord, his appearance in Old French romance and later in Boccaccio's Decameron, and Dante placing him among the virtuous non-Christians in the first circle of Hell. A Muslim enemy was absorbed into Christendom's own ideal of the noble ruler.
entries.note: Jubb, 'The Legend of Saladin in Western Literature and Historiography' (2000); Tolan, 'Sons of Ishmael' (2008), ch. on the Saladin legend.

entries.label: The Frankish–Ayyubid truce system
entries.hint: The Ayyubids institutionalised coexistence with the Frankish coast: multi-year truces renewed almost as routine, villages whose revenue was formally split between the two sides, and safe-conducts for pilgrims and caravans. For al-Adil and al-Kamil a stable, trading Frankish coast was frequently preferable to provoking a new crusade.
entries.note: Köhler, 'Alliances and Treaties between Frankish and Muslim Rulers in the Middle East' (Eng. trans. 2013); Holt, 'Early Mamluk Diplomacy' (1995), for the treaty forms that carried over.

entries.label: The scholars fleeing the Mongols
entries.hint: The destruction of Khwarazm, and then of Baghdad in 1258, drove astronomers, physicians, metalworkers and jurists westward into Ayyubid Syria and Egypt. With Mamluk Cairo after them, these lands became the refuge and the archive of the eastern Islamic learned tradition.
entries.note: the migrations are traced through the biographical dictionaries (Ibn Abi Usaybia; later Ibn Khallikan); Yaqut and the Mosul metalworkers are documented cases. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

entries.label: Al-Kamil and Frederick II
entries.hint: Years of correspondence — Frederick sent philosophical and mathematical questions, answered by scholars in the sultan's circle — an exchange of gifts including exotic animals and an astronomical tent, and finally the 1229 treaty that returned Jerusalem without a battle. The regard between the sultan and the excommunicate emperor scandalised the clergy of both faiths.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil, who later served as al-Zahir Baybars' envoy to Frederick's son Manfred; Abulafia, 'Frederick II: A Medieval Emperor' (1988), ch. 6.

entries.label: The Mongol ultimatum
entries.hint: Mongol envoys demanded the submission of the Jaziran and Syrian Ayyubid princes. Some sent tribute, some resisted, and al-Nasir Yusuf tried to negotiate a middle course. The fall of the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dagh in 1243 removed the northern buffer and forced the choice on every ruler between the Taurus and Egypt.
entries.note: Bar Hebraeus; the Mongol demands as reported in Juvayni and in the Armenian chronicler Kirakos. Jackson, 'The Mongols and the Islamic World' (2017), ch. 4.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Egypt and Syria under one hand, Outremer reduced to a coast, Egypt recognised as the key to the Levant, the Mongol shadow, and the Mamluk seizure

entries.label: Egypt and Syria under one hand
entries.hint: For the first time since the 10th century a single Sunni authority — loose, but real — spanned Egypt, Muslim Syria and the Jazira, aligned with the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. It was the strategic encirclement of the Crusader states that made Hattin possible.
entries.note: Humphreys, 'From Saladin to the Mongols' (1977); Lyons and Jackson, 'Saladin' (1982), on the deliberate construction of the bloc before the 1187 offensive.

entries.label: Outremer reduced to a coast
entries.hint: The Third Crusade recovered a coastal strip but never the interior. For the next century the Frankish Levant was a chain of fortified port cities living on trade and truces — no longer a territorial kingdom. That was the settlement the Ayyubids on the whole preferred to maintain rather than eliminate.
entries.note: Prawer, 'The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem' (1972); the shift from an agrarian kingdom to a mercantile enclave is the theme of much subsequent Crusader-states scholarship.

entries.label: Egypt bound into the Mediterranean economy
entries.hint: The Italian treaties, the alum, sugar and spice trades and the funduq system tied Ayyubid Egypt structurally to Venice, Pisa and Genoa. The commercial relationship outlived the dynasty by three centuries and shaped the Mamluk and then the Ottoman Mediterranean.
entries.note: Ashtor, 'Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages' (1983); Jacoby's studies. The structural continuity across the 1250 dynastic break is the point.

entries.label: Egypt is the key to the Levant
entries.hint: The Fifth Crusade and the Seventh Crusade both struck at Egypt, not at Jerusalem, on the recognition that whoever held the Nile could not be dislodged from Syria. Both broke at Mansura. The second brought down the dynasty that had beaten it.
entries.note: Powell, 'Anatomy of a Crusade' (1986); Jordan, 'Louis IX and the Challenge of the Crusade' (1979). The strategic logic was stated openly in the Crusade planning literature.

entries.label: The Mongol shadow
entries.hint: Chinggis Khan's destruction of the Khwarazmian empire in 1219–21 sent the shock west: the stateless Khwarazmian cavalry became a wrecking force for hire — it was they who sacked Jerusalem in 1244 — and the Mongols themselves reached the Ayyubid world through the Seljuk collapse at Köse Dagh in 1243.
entries.note: Jackson, 'The Mongols and the Islamic World' (2017); the Khwarazmian mercenaries' path from Iran to Palestine is traced by Jackson in BSOAS (1987). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

entries.label: The Mamluks take Egypt
entries.hint: The Bahriyya regiment's murder of Turanshah put a self-perpetuating corps of freed slave-soldiers in charge of the richest state in the region. Within a decade they had stopped the Mongols at Ayn Jalut and absorbed Ayyubid Syria. The confederation was over — except for Hama, left to its Ayyubid prince as a Mamluk vassal until 1341.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil; al-Maqrizi. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's entries on the Ayyubid–Mamluk transition and on the slave-supply that made it possible; the Mamluk Sultanate itself belongs to a folio still to be built (mamluks-1250-1517).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The one woman to rule medieval Egypt, the princess-builders of Syria, the slave regiments before the coup, the Coptic community under pressure, and the beloved youth in Ayyubid letters

entries.label: The Coptic community under pressure
entries.hint: The Ayyubid century brought episodic dress edicts, dismissals of Coptic officials, and a wave of pressure in the 1250s — even as Copto-Arabic scholarship reached its height. Conversion to Islam accelerated among the administrative families; the long demographic decline of Egyptian Christianity is usually dated from about here.
entries.note: the 'History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria' (contemporary); el-Leithy, 'Coptic Culture and Conversion in Medieval Cairo 1293–1524' (PhD 2005), for the slightly later acceleration and its Ayyubid roots.

entries.label: The slave supply of Egypt
entries.loc: Cairo; the Nile; the Red Sea; the Black Sea
entries.hint: Enslaved people reached Egypt down the Nile from Nubia, across the Red Sea from the Horn, across the Mediterranean from Europe, and increasingly across the Black Sea from the Qipchaq steppe — the last stream furnishing the Turkish military slaves. Domestic slavery fills the Geniza's contracts; eunuchs staffed the Citadel; the trade would supply the folio's own successor ruling class.
entries.note: the Geniza on household slavery (Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society' vol. 1); the Black Sea military-slave route matured under the Mamluks and drew in Genoese and Venetian shipping — flag the Mamluk folio.

entries.label: The beloved youth in Ayyubid letters
entries.hint: The poetry and adab of the Ayyubid courts — Baha al-Din Zuhayr, the anthologists — carry on the long convention of the love lyric addressed to a beautiful youth (the ghulam, the amrad), alongside the jurists' flat condemnation of the act itself. The distance between a celebrated literary sensibility and the letter of the law is characteristic of the period.
entries.note: the diwan of Baha al-Din Zuhayr; the broader convention in Wright and Rowson (eds.), 'Homoeroticism in Classical Arabic Literature' (1997). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio and the Islamic Eastern Arabia folio's ghulam entry.

entries.label: The princess-builders of Ayyubid Syria
entries.hint: Dayfa Khatun, granddaughter of Saladin's brother, governed Aleppo as regent from 1236 to 1242 and founded two great khanqahs. Other Ayyubid women — Rabia Khatun, Zumurrud Khatun — endowed madrasas and tomb-complexes across Damascus. The religious endowment was the channel through which elite women exercised durable public agency.
entries.note: Eddé, 'La principauté ayyoubide d'Alep' (1999), on Dayfa Khatun; Humphreys, 'Women as Patrons of Religious Architecture in Ayyubid Damascus', Muqarnas (1994), catalogues the foundations.

entries.label: The mamluk regiments before the coup
entries.hint: The Bahriyya — al-Salih Ayyub's regiment of purchased Qipchaq Turks, quartered in a new barracks on Rawda island in the Nile — together with the earlier Salihiyya and Asadiyya corps: slave households bought as boys, trained and manumitted together, that developed a corporate identity and a political will years before they seized the state in 1250.
entries.note: Ayalon, 'Le régiment Bahriya dans l'armée mamelouke', REI (1951), and 'The Mamluk Novice', in his collected studies; Humphreys (1977) on the Ayyubid military households. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio's mamluk-household entry.

entries.label: Shajar al-Durr
entries.hint: The Turkic slave-concubine of al-Salih Ayyub concealed his death to keep the army together against Louis IX, then in 1250 was proclaimed sultana of Egypt in her own name, with coins struck and the Friday prayer read for her — the only woman to rule medieval Egypt outright. Pressed to take a male co-ruler, she married the Mamluk Aybak, had him killed in 1257 when he sought another wife, and was beaten to death days later.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil and al-Maqrizi; her coins survive. Duncan, 'Scholarly Views of Shajar al-Durr', Al-Masaq (2000), on how the male chroniclers framed her.
